prompt_payload.task: Design a diverse library of executable semantic optimization skills for finite-pool scientific search. Each skill defines interpretable rule features plus a conservative Bayesian linear surrogate blended with strong target-only GP-UCB and GP-EI anchors.

target.title: Matbench refractive-index replay
target.boundary: Field values and counts are public; target outcomes are not included.

source_transfer_evidence.boundary: Only source identity, objective, and public source-target field alignment are provided. Source outcomes, effects, support counts, and value priors are withheld.

executor.semantic_model: Rules become binary features. Revealed target outcomes fit a ridge Bayesian linear surrogate whose coefficient prior follows rule weights.
executor.anchor: A rank blend of target-only GP-UCB and GP-EI.
executor.fusion: semantic_mass_start/end controls the rank mass assigned to the semantic surrogate; the remaining mass stays on the target-only anchor.
executor.selection: Independent calibration seeds select one frozen skill. Independent held-out seeds are evaluated only after selection.

design_requirements: Use only exact field/value pairs in public_semantic_fields.

Each conditions object must map a real catalog field name directly to one exact catalog value, for example {"dominant_family": "oxide"}. Never use literal placeholder keys such as exact_field, field_name, field, or value.
Give every skill a distinct, descriptive scientific skill_id. Never copy schema placeholders such as short_unique_name or add numeric suffixes to a placeholder.
Give every skill 3-10 rules; use two-condition interactions only when scientifically meaningful.
Include at least one conservative low-semantic-mass skill.
Include at least one skill grounded only in the supplied source-target field alignment; do not imply that source outcome effects were observed.
Include at least one domain-knowledge skill.
Include a counter-hypothesis skill that reverses or downweights an uncertain source relation.
Prefer mechanistic, chemically or physically interpretable rules over arbitrary coverage rules.
Use positive weights for conditions expected to improve the target objective and negative weights for risks.
Do not claim access to target outcomes and do not output candidate identifiers.

rules.rationale: short scientific rationale

skills.hypothesis: what this skill transfers and when it may fail

cards.summary: For real_matbench_phonons, use the LLM-defined maximize_light_nonmetal_phonon_response partition to choose the initial batch, then continue with the target-only optimizer.

cards.title: Layered transferable skill artifact
cards.summary: CARE 2.0 skill transfer should not be limited to acquisition-level score adjustment; a reusable skill should specify representation mapping, mechanism hypothesis, model binding, acquisition binding, gate/risk checks, and workflow boundaries.
cards.content: A layered transferable skill artifact records six linked layers. Representation layer: what source fields or descriptors can be mapped to the target task. Mechanism layer: what scientific hypothesis is being reused, such as role importance, descriptor relevance, solvation, sterics, electronics, or stability. Model layer: how the skill changes a surrogate model, embedding, kernel, feature transform, or uncertainty prior. Acquisition layer: how it changes candidate ranking, UCB/EI, exploration strength, or candidate filtering. Gate/risk layer: when the transfer is allowed, when it should be rejected, and what negative-transfer failure modes are known. Workflow layer: experiment constraints, budget, batch design, data reveal protocol, and audit outputs. This card is the intended CARE 2.0 abstraction behind the current transfer-weighted kernel experiments.

care_knowledge_context.instruction: Use these public, previously archived cards only as reusable design lessons. Do not copy reported target values into a rule and do not imply that the current target outcomes were observed. Prefer lessons that survived held-out calibration.

rules.rationale: Oxides often exhibit high electronic polarizability and wide band gaps, favoring high refractive index.
Absence of transition metals reduces optical absorption losses, beneficial for refractive index.
Balanced elemental fractions promote structural stability and uniform polarizability.

skills.hypothesis: Transfers the hypothesis that oxide anions and absence of transition metals favor high refractive index; may fail for high-density chalcogenides or materials with strong ionic character.

rules.rationale: Chalcogenides (S, Se, Te) have high polarizability due to large atomic radii, potentially increasing refractive index.
Higher mean atomic number increases electron density, enhancing electronic polarizability.
Transition metals can contribute d-electron polarizability, but risk absorption; cautious positive weight.

skills.hypothesis: Transfers the hypothesis that chalcogenides and high atomic number elements boost refractive index via polarizability; may fail if absorption from transition metals dominates.

rules.rationale: Conservative weight based solely on source-target field alignment for anion_family, no outcome assumption.
Conservative weight based solely on source-target field alignment for dominant_family, no outcome assumption.
Conservative weight based solely on source-target field alignment for element_count_bin, no outcome assumption.

skills.hypothesis: Grounded only in supplied source-target field alignment; transfers no source outcome effects, highly conservative; likely fails if alignment does not correlate with target mechanism.

rules.rationale: Halides typically have low polarizability and refractive index due to small, electronegative anions.
Binary compounds may lack compositional complexity needed for high refractive index tuning.

skills.hypothesis: Minimal semantic influence with strong anchor reliance; transfers cautious avoidance of halides and binaries; may fail if exceptions exist (e.g., heavy halides).

rules.rationale: Pnictides (N, P, As) can form covalent networks with high polarizability, beneficial for refractive index.
Moderate atomic number balances electron density and band gap for optimal refractive index.
Absence of lanthanides reduces f-electron absorption losses, favoring high refractive index.
Concentrated elemental fractions may increase density and polarizability, but risk phase instability.

skills.hypothesis: Transfers domain knowledge that pnictides, moderate atomic number, and no lanthanides favor high refractive index; may fail for materials where high density leads to absorption or instability.

rules.rationale: Counter to common assumption, heavy halides (e.g., iodides) may exhibit high polarizability; downweight due to uncertainty.
Source relation uncertain; downweight transition metals due to potential absorption risks outweighing benefits.
High element count may enable refractive index tuning, but effect uncertain; cautious positive weight.

skills.hypothesis: Reverses or downweights uncertain source relations (e.g., halides negative, transition metals positive); transfers skepticism; may fail if source correlations hold in target.

rules.rationale: Oxides combine ionic and covalent bonding, enhancing electronic polarizability and refractive index.
Alkaline earth cations (e.g., Ba, Sr) have high polarizability, beneficial for refractive index.
Low mean atomic number may correlate with wide band gaps, reducing absorption for refractive index.
Interaction: Oxide anions with alkaline earth cations may synergistically enhance polarizability and refractive index.

skills.hypothesis: Transfers the hypothesis that ionic-covalent balance (oxides with alkaline earth) favors high refractive index; may fail for highly ionic or covalent extremes.

rules.rationale: Very high mean atomic number maximizes electron density and polarizability, potentially yielding high refractive index.
Lanthanides introduce f-electron absorption risks, which may reduce refractive index effectiveness.
Dominant heavy elements increase density and polarizability, but may lead to instability or absorption.
Interaction: Very high atomic number with lanthanides compounds absorption risks, strongly negative.

skills.hypothesis: Transfers the hypothesis that heavy elements boost refractive index but lanthanides pose absorption risks; may fail if lanthanide contributions are beneficial or heavy elements cause instability.
